name: Dalabon
confidence_why: The initial-stress rule rests only on Capell's 1962 handbook sketch, while Sandefur and Jentian 1977 put primary stress on the penultimate syllable with secondary stress on the initial, Evans, Fletcher and Ross 2008 describe stress on the first syllable of every morpheme-based foot with no fixed main-stress position, and Torres and Babinski 2024 find no acoustic evidence of lexical stress in nouns at all.
catalog_quote: Main stress falls on the initial syllable, secondary stress on alternate syllables thereafter. The final syllable in odd-syllabled words is never stressed. (Hayes 1993:175)
sweep_summary: Both works with stress in the title are the same paper (Glottolog duplicate records): Fletcher, Evans & Ross 2004 'Pausing strategies and prosodic boundaries in Dalabon', SST 2004 pp. 436-439. The live ASSTA site no longer serves the 2004 proceedings; I recovered the archived proceedings index (paper) and the PDF from the the Internet Archive (archive.org was intermittently offline; a retry loop got it) and saved it with a text. It is a pause/boundary study: p. 437 says phrasal prominence falls on the IP-final, penultimate or antepenultimate syllable 'depending on the location of lexical stress (Fletcher & Evans 2002)' but states no word-stress rule — silent on the catalog's classification. Beyond the listed items this search of works with stress in the title obtained two further open first-hand sources from ANU Open Research: Evans, Fletcher & Ross 2008 (Linguistics 46; p. 102: stress is a series of stressed foot-initial syllables, feet built over morphemes, relative prominence set intonationally rather than by word position; prefixes primary, disyllabic clitics secondary) and Fletcher, Evans & Ross 2005 (DiSS; feet over morphemes, no stress rule). Fletcher & Evans 2002 (JIPA; abstract only, Cambridge paywall, Minerva bitstream could not be reached by automated download) and Fletcher 2014 (OUP chapter, paywalled) remain the two high-priority unread items; Jepson & Ennever 2023 medium. Re-reading the on-disk material: Capell 1962:93 (the deciding source) gives initial stress with exceptions (final glottalised consonant, future suffix) that the Hayes-regularised catalog string drops; Sandefur & Jentian 1977:63 gives penultimate primary with initial secondary; Ross 2003:12-13 finds prefix stress and inconsistent placement in verbs; Ross 2011:59 is silent; Torres & Babinski 2024 find no acoustic lexical stress in nouns. Net: the fixed-strict initial-primary coding is contradicted by every post-1962 first-hand source read; EFR 2008 p. 102 is the best new statement and should supersede Capell/Hayes as the deciding source, with the reclassify already proposed by the 2026-09-16 check.

new_statements.quote: Stress, though assigned over the whole grammatical word, takes the form of a number of stressed foot-initial syllables, whose relative prominence is determined by higher level intonational factors rather than positioning with respect to the word boundary, so one cannot use location of "primary stress" as a way of locating phonological word boundaries.
new_statements.citation: Evans, Nicholas, Janet Fletcher & Belinda Ross (2008). Big words, small phrases: Mismatches between pause units and the polysynthetic word in Dalabon. Linguistics 46(1): 89-129.
new_statements.locator: p. 102, section 5 'Problems in delineating the phonological word' (supporting passages p. 99 s.4 and p. 100)
new_statements.reading: The language's principal researchers, writing from fieldwork and a ToBI-annotated corpus, describe Dalabon word stress as a sequence of stressed foot-initial syllables with feet built over morphemes (bimoraic minimum), pronominal prefixes taking primary and disyllabic clitics secondary stress; which foot head is most prominent is fixed by intonation, not by distance from the word edge. This is not a fixed-strict initial-primary alternating system: the catalog's Hayes-regularised Capell string (initial primary, alternating secondary, final never stressed) is contradicted on primary-stress placement, and the dedicated SIL phonology held by the project (Sandefur & Jentian 1977:63, penultimate primary + initial secondary) and the only acoustic test (Torres & Babinski 2024, no acoustic lexical stress in nouns) point the same way. The prior check's reclassify (drop strict, mark primary placement contested, add contra entries) stands; the FER 2004 title that triggered this search of works with stress in the title adds nothing on word-stress placement.

audit.recode_to: Drop 'fixed-strict' (not in the strict set) and mark primary-stress placement as contested: keep the left-edge trochaic rhythm that Capell 1962 and Sandefur & Jentian 1977 share (10, 1010-type prominence on syllables 1 and 3) but record that S&J 1977:63 and the Evans/Fletcher school place PRIMARY on the penult with initial secondary (10, 100~010, 1010 [primary syll 3], 10010 — vs coded 10100), that Evans-Fletcher-Ross 2008:102 say relative prominence among foot heads is intonational not word-positional, and that Torres & Babinski 2024 find no acoustic lexical stress at all. Add contra entries (S&J 1977:63; T&B 2024:1058) and a caution; if the catalog has a 'phrasal prominence / lexical stress doubtful' class, Dalabon is a candidate pending Fletcher 2014.

sources.citation: Evans, Nicholas, Janet Fletcher & Belinda Ross (2008). Big words, small phrases: Mismatches between pause units and the polysynthetic word in Dalabon. Linguistics 46(1): 89-129. doi:10.1515/LING.2008.004
sources.quote: p. 102: Stress, though assigned over the whole grammatical word, takes the form of a number of stressed foot-initial syllables, whose relative prominence is determined by higher level intonational factors rather than positioning with respect to the word boundary, so one cannot use location of "primary stress" as a way of locating phonological word boundaries. — p. 99: if disyllabic (e.g., ablative =walûng or 3plO bulu=) they normally take secondary stress on their first syllable, but they cannot take primary stress. — p. 100: the object pronoun takes its own secondary stress but is rhythmically integrated with the following verb, whose prefix also takes its own primary stress, e.g., bùlubúlah-nan
sources.locator: p. 102, section 5 'Problems in delineating the phonological word'; also p. 99 (section 4, clitics), p. 100 (object proclitics), p. 103 s.5.1 and fn. 15 (feet built over morphemes, bimoraic minimum)
sources.note: First-hand description by the language's principal researchers (fieldwork + ToBI-annotated corpus): stress is assigned over the whole grammatical word as a series of stressed foot-initial syllables; feet are constructed over morphemes with a bimoraic minimum (s.5.1, fn. 15); which foot head carries 'primary' prominence is decided by intonation, not by position relative to the word edge. Pronominal prefixes carry primary stress and disyllabic clitics secondary stress on their first syllable. sources.citation: Ross, Belinda (2003). The phonological/grammatical mismatch in the Dalabon word: a phonetic study. Honours thesis, Department of Linguistics and Applied Linguistics, University of Melbourne.
sources.quote: A pronominal prefix in Dalabon always receives stress placement – typically primary stress, however secondary stress is also seen. ... The basic possibilities for stress placement of the verbal word in Dalabon is illustrated in 8) to 10) above. A single phonological word may thus receive one or more stresses. However, pronominal prefixes always attract at least a secondary stress. As stress placement within the verbal word in Dalabon is inconsistent, the prosodic feature stress does not assist in defining the phonological word.
sources.note: Instrumental (RMS) study of verbal words: prefixes always stressed (usually primary), 'almost every syllable of every foot receives stress' in some words, and placement within the verbal word is inconsistent — no fixed word-edge rule.

sources.citation: Capell, A. 1962. Some Linguistic Types in Australia (Handbook of Australian Languages, Part 2). Oceania Linguistic Monographs 7. Sydney: University of Sydney. Dalabon sketch, p. 93, s.1.4 'Stress' (archive.org Rosetta Project item rosettaproject_ngk_phon-2, 4-page extract).
sources.quote: 'i. In words of two syllables, stress falls on the first ... ii. In words of three syllables, stress is normally on the first ... iii. In three syllable words a final glottalised consonant tends to attract the stress ... iv. In words of more than three syllables, a secondary stress may occur in the third syllable ... v. Final stress occurs on the future suffix -jan ... Dr. West ... did not hear this type of stress; it may be purely eastern.'
sources.note: Impressionistic 1962 sketch: initial stress in 2-3 syllable words, 'may' have secondary stress on the third syllable in longer words, but with exceptions (final glottalised consonant attracts stress; final stress on the future suffix). The catalog quote (via Hayes 1993:175) regularises this into a strict alternating initial-primary pattern and drops Capell's exceptions.

sources.citation: Ross, Belinda. 2011. Prosody and grammar in Dalabon and Kayardild. PhD thesis, University of Melbourne (open, minerva-access handle 11343/36303; bitstream).
sources.quote: No word-stress rule is stated. p.59: 'Stress assignment likewise does not assist in determining the boundaries of prosodic units. The few fast speech assimilations that are found occur in larger domains such as the IP as defined by pause and rhythm.' IP labelling: 'a high pitch accent is realised for the most part as a pitch peak on the penultimate or antepenultimate syllable of an IP.' Treats prominence as phrasal; silent on the coded initial-primary word rule.
sources.note: 75-minute ToBI-annotated Dalabon corpus study by the third author of Evans-Fletcher-Ross 2008; downloaded now — it treats prominence as IP-level (H* on IP penult/antepenult) and gives no word-stress rule, so it bounds what the Melbourne group claims about lexical stress.

sources.citation: Fletcher, Janet, Nicholas Evans & Belinda Ross (2005). The intra-word pause and disfluency in Dalabon. Proceedings of DiSS'05, Disfluency in Spontaneous Speech Workshop, Aix-en-Provence, 10-12 Sept 2005, pp. 77-81.
sources.quote: The two relevant phonological requirements that must be met before pause can occur are that (a) This must not split a foot, though since feet are constructed over morphemes in virtually all cases, this could also be phrased as a morphological requirement. Because feet have a bimoraic minimum, this effectively means that the prefix must be closed, if monosyllabic, and otherwise satisfy a disyllabic minimum (b) The remainder of the word must have at least two syllables.
sources.note: Pause/disfluency study; only prosodic-structure statement is that feet are built over morphemes with a bimoraic minimum. No word-stress placement rule; the word 'stress' does not occur in the paper.

sources.citation: Fletcher, Janet, Nicholas Evans & Belinda Ross (2004). Pausing strategies and prosodic boundaries in Dalabon. Proceedings of the 10th Australian International Conference on Speech Science and Technology (SST 2004), Macquarie University, Sydney, 8-10 Dec 2004, pp. 436-439. [Glottolog id 305093]
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: not located online or in the libraries checked
sources.quote: With respect to phrasal stress and intonation in Dalabon, our earlier studies suggest that phrasal stress or prominence (that is, the most intonationally prominent syllable in a phrase) tends to be located on the final, penultimate, or antepenultimate syllable of intonational phrases depending on the location of lexical stress (Fletcher & Evans, 2002). Due to its polysynthetic morphology, Dalabon also has extremely long words consisting of several morphemes. As a consequence, grammatical words are often realized as one, two or in certain rare cases, three intonational phrases.
sources.note: A 4-page instrumental study of silent-pause placement and prosodic boundaries (ToBI break indices) in Dalabon narrative. It presupposes that Dalabon has lexical stress and says phrasal prominence sits on the IP-final, penultimate or antepenultimate syllable 'depending on the location of lexical stress', but it states no rule for where word stress falls; the only other stress mention is vowel reduction of /e/,/i/ 'in some unstressed positions' (p. 437).

sources.note: The current authoritative description of Dalabon prosody by the phonetician who has worked on the language since 2000; per Torres & Babinski 2024 it states the working stress rule (penultimate primary, initial secondary, bimoraic syllables attract stress) that the Melbourne group uses — the one unread document that decides between our Capell/Hayes initial-primary coding and the Sandefur & Jentian penultimate rule. sources.quote: Both languages have also previously been described as having lexical stress. In this study, the acoustic correlates of syllables associated with intonational pitch accents, were measured, namely, F0, duration, RMS amplitude and vowel quality, in one lengthy narrative text from each language. ... Results indicate that syllables associated with pitch accents are phonetically lengthened and have marginally higher RMS amplitude.
sources.note: Abstract only: the first instrumental study of Dalabon prominence; it treats lexical stress as previously described and measures pitch-accented syllables. FER 2004:437 cites it for the claim that phrasal prominence falls on IP-final/penult/antepenult 'depending on the location of lexical stress', so the body presumably states which syllables count as lexically stressed. Not readable openly.
